title: Path traversal in theme-background DELETE allows deleting any server-writable file
scenario: A logged-in user deletes arbitrary files anywhere the server process can write (other users' uploads, logs, the SQLite DB, ...), causing data loss / DoS.
evidence: DELETE /api/user/themes/background/theme-bg-..%2f..%2f..%2f..%2ftmp%2f...%2fSENTINEL.txt -> 200 OK, and a sentinel file created outside /uploads was deleted (verified: fs.existsSync -> false).
test: tests/attacks/upload.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Dateien anderer Nutzer oder des Servers loeschen › Pfad-Traversal im fileRef darf keine Datei ausserhalb von /uploads loeschen
cause: server/routes/themes.ts:136 the only safety check is fileRef.startsWith('theme-bg-'); 'theme-bg-../../..' satisfies it. server/routes/themes.ts:155 path.join('./uploads', fileRef) then resolves outside the uploads folder. Express decodes %2F in the single :fileRef segment back to '/'.
fix: Reject any fileRef containing '/', '\\' or '..' (or validate with /^theme-bg-[\w.-]+$/), and verify path.resolve(UPLOADS_DIR, fileRef) still starts with UPLOADS_DIR + path.sep before unlinking.

title: Missing file-ownership check lets a user delete another user's uploaded background
scenario: A logged-in attacker who knows/guesses another user's theme-background file name (it is returned in a public /uploads URL) deletes that victim's file.
evidence: Victim uploads bg -> fileRef theme-bg-....png (exists on disk). Attacker (different account) DELETE /api/user/themes/background/<victim fileRef> -> 200 OK, victim's file removed (fs.existsSync -> false).
test: tests/attacks/upload.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Dateien anderer Nutzer oder des Servers loeschen › ein Nutzer darf das Hintergrundbild eines anderen Nutzers nicht loeschen
cause: server/routes/themes.ts:141-158 the 'isReferenced' guard only checks whether the CALLER's own themes reference the file; it never checks that the file belongs to the caller, so any authenticated user can delete any theme-bg file.
fix: Bind uploaded background files to their owner (e.g. store ownerId, or prefix the filename with the user id) and refuse deletion unless the caller owns the file.

title: Decompression/pixel bomb: huge-dimension images decoded without an input-pixel limit
scenario: A logged-in user uploads a tiny, highly-compressible image with enormous pixel dimensions; the server fully decodes it, burning CPU and large amounts of memory (potential OOM under concurrency).
evidence: A 776 KB 16000x16000 PNG (256 MP) uploaded as theme background -> 200 OK after ~63s of processing; a 202 KB 8000x8000 PNG (64 MP) -> 200 OK after ~13s. The server never rejects oversized dimensions.
test: tests/attacks/upload.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Server mit einer Bild-Bombe lahmlegen › riesige Pixel-Dimensionen muessen beim Theme-Background schnell abgelehnt werden; … › riesige Pixel-Dimensionen muessen bei Post-Medien schnell abgelehnt werden
cause: server/utils/file-upload.ts:66 sanitizeImage() calls sharp(filepath) with no limitInputPixels, so sharp's ~268 MP default applies (decoding ~268 MP RGB needs ~800 MB RAM). Used by server/routes/posts.ts:122 and server/routes/themes.ts:112. processProfileImage (file-upload.ts:205) caps at 100 MP, which is still very large.
fix: Pass a strict limitInputPixels (e.g. 24-50 MP) to every sharp() call and read metadata() first to reject oversized width*height before decoding; lower the limit on processProfileImage too.

title: Rejected uploads leave orphan files on disk (no cleanup on early returns)
scenario: A logged-in user repeatedly submits posts with media that is rejected after multer has written the file (moderation block, post cooldown, category/community errors); each rejected request leaves a file on disk, letting the attacker fill the disk despite the cooldown.
evidence: Post with content 'this is porn content' + image -> 400 CONTENT_BLOCKED, image file remains in /uploads (1 new orphan). Second post within cooldown -> 429 POST_COOLDOWN, image file remains in /uploads (1 new orphan). Neither path deletes req.files.
test: tests/attacks/upload.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Festplatte mit Waisen-Dateien fluten › ein durch Moderation abgelehnter Post darf keine Waisen-Datei hinterlassen; … › ein durch Cooldown abgelehnter Post darf keine Waisen-Datei hinterlassen
cause: server/routes/posts.ts:21 postUpload.any() writes the file to disk first; the cooldown return (posts.ts:44-49), moderation return (posts.ts:83-86), category return (posts.ts:70-74) and 'community not found' (posts.ts:77) all return before the file is ever written to a post and never unlink req.files.
fix: Validate cooldown/moderation/category BEFORE accepting the file, or wrap the handler so any non-201 response unlinks every file in req.files (finally block).

title: No per-user upload quota or count limit (disk-exhaustion hardening)
scenario: A logged-in user uploads an unbounded number of files (theme backgrounds have no cooldown at all; profile/post media only have per-file size limits), eventually filling the disk.
evidence: Code review: the three multer configs in server/utils/file-upload.ts set only per-file 'limits.fileSize' (50/5/10 MB) and (profile) files:1. There is no per-user storage quota, no cap on number of stored files, and no rate limit on /api/user/themes/background. Combined with ATK-UPLOAD-4 orphans, a single account can write unbounded data.
test: tests/attacks/upload.attack.test.ts › Angriff: Festplatte mit Waisen-Dateien fluten (orphan tests demonstrate the uncapped-write primitive)
cause: server/utils/file-upload.ts:120,153,187 only per-file size limits exist; no quota accounting anywhere; POST /api/user/themes/background has no rate limiter (server/routes/themes.ts:94).
fix: Add a per-user storage quota and/or max file count, and a rate limiter on the upload routes (especially theme backgrounds).

title: Uploaded GIFs are stored byte-for-byte (not re-encoded); metadata and polyglot payloads persist
scenario: An attacker uploads a valid-header GIF carrying an HTML/JS polyglot or metadata payload as post media; it is stored verbatim on the app origin. It is NOT served as active HTML (see note), but the raw payload persists.
route: POST /api/posts (and POST /api/user/themes/background, which also accept image/gif)
evidence: A GIF89a header + '<html><script>/*ATK_POLYGLOT_SCRIPT*/alert(1)</script></html>' uploaded as image/gif -> 201; the stored file still contains the raw marker ATK_POLYGLOT_SCRIPT. Mitigated at serve time: GET /uploads/<file>.gif returns Content-Type image/gif + X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so it cannot be interpreted as a document.
test: tests/attacks/upload.attack.test.ts › Angriff: aktives Script ueber einen Upload ausliefern › ein GIF-Polyglot wird nicht als aktives HTML ausgeliefert (und sollte re-encoded werden)
cause: server/utils/file-upload.ts:56-59 sanitizeImage() returns early for GIFs (only .jpg/.jpeg/.png/.webp are re-encoded); the signature check (file-upload.ts:19) only validates the first bytes, so trailing/metadata bytes survive unchanged.
fix: Re-encode GIFs too (sharp can transcode animated GIFs) or strip them to a safe canonical form; at minimum this removes embedded payloads and EXIF/XMP from GIF uploads.

title: Post images keep their original extension while their bytes are re-encoded to WebP
scenario: Not directly exploitable, but a JPEG/PNG post image is stored under a .jpg/.png name whose bytes are actually WebP, so the served Content-Type (derived from extension) does not match the real content.
evidence: Code review: sanitizeImage writes WebP bytes to '.sanitized' then renames over the original '.jpg'/'.png' path, keeping the extension; express.static then serves it as image/jpeg/png. nosniff is set and rendering still works, so there is no security impact, only a Content-Type/content mismatch.
test: (code evidence only; no dedicated failing test)
cause: server/utils/file-upload.ts:62-75 sanitizeImage keeps the original filename/extension deliberately so existing references stay valid, but converts the bytes to WebP.
fix: Either keep the real format when re-encoding, or rename the stored file to .webp and update the post's mediaUrl accordingly.
